subject: Fysik
title: Electricity and magnetism
sourceSummary: Current, voltage and resistance, series versus parallel circuits, and the basics of magnetism and electromagnetism.

questions.prompt: What is measured in the unit ampere (A)?
questions.opener: Ampere is the unit for one of the three basic electrical quantities: current, voltage and resistance.
choices: Voltage
Resistance
Electric current
Power
questions.explanation: Ampere (A) is the unit of electric current, that is, the amount of charge passing per second. Voltage is measured in volts (V) and resistance in ohms (Ω).

questions.prompt: A circuit has a voltage of 12 V and a resistance of 4 Ω. What is the current, according to Ohm's law (U = R · I)?
questions.opener: Solve for I in the formula: I = U / R.
choices: 3 A
8 A
questions.explanation: I = U / R = 12 V / 4 Ω = 3 A. Multiplying 12 by 4 instead gives the incorrect answer of 48.

questions.prompt: What does resistance (measured in ohms) describe?
questions.opener: Think about what happens when a wire or component makes it harder for the current to flow.
choices: How much energy is stored in a component
How much a component resists or "slows down" the electric current
How fast the current moves through the circuit
How many electrons there are in the circuit in total
questions.explanation: Resistance is a measure of how much a conductor or component opposes the current. High resistance, at the same voltage, gives a lower current (according to Ohm's law I = U/R).

questions.prompt: Two lamps are connected in series to a battery. What happens if one lamp breaks (the circuit is interrupted)?
questions.opener: In a series circuit, there is only one single path for the current to take.
choices: Only the broken lamp goes out, the other one shines as usual
Both lamps go out because the current path is broken
The other lamp shines more brightly
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: In a series circuit, the current flows in a single closed loop through all the components. If one lamp breaks, the whole circuit is interrupted and current cannot flow anywhere, so both lamps go out.

questions.prompt: Why are the lamps in a house normally connected in parallel and not in series?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to the rest of the lamps if a single lamp goes out or is switched off.
choices: A parallel connection allows each lamp to be switched on and off independently of the others
A parallel connection draws less current overall
A parallel connection means the lamps can never break
There is no advantage, it's just a tradition
questions.explanation: In a parallel connection, each lamp has its own current path, so if one lamp goes out or is switched off, the others continue to shine as usual. This is why household outlets and lamps are connected in parallel.

questions.prompt: What happens if you pass a current through a coil of wire?
questions.opener: A moving electric charge always creates something around it that can affect other magnets.
choices: Nothing in particular, the wire just gets warm
A magnetic field is created around the coil, an electromagnet
The coil becomes permanently magnetic forever
The current is converted directly into light
questions.explanation: A current through a conductor creates a magnetic field, and if the wire is wound into a coil the field is strengthened — you get an electromagnet. Unlike a permanent magnet, the field disappears when the current is switched off.

questions.prompt: A lamp is connected to a voltage of 9 V and the resistance in the circuit is 3 Ω. Calculate the current through the lamp using Ohm's law.
questions.opener: Ohm's law: U = R · I. Solve for I and substitute the known values.
steps: Start from Ohm's law: U = R · I.
Solve for the current: I = U / R.
Substitute the values: I = 9 V / 3 Ω.

questions.prompt: Summarise the basic concepts of current, voltage, resistance, Ohm's law, series/parallel circuits and electromagnetism.
questions.opener: Go through one quantity at a time and link them with Ohm's law before turning the card over.
questions.answer: Current (I), measured in amperes (A): the amount of charge flowing per second · Voltage (U), measured in volts (V): the "driving force" that makes the current flow · Resistance (R), measured in ohms (Ω): the opposition that slows down the current · Ohm's law: U = R · I, the relationship between voltage, resistance and current · Series circuit: the components sit one after another in a single current path — if one component breaks, the whole circuit is interrupted · Parallel circuit: the components each have their own current path — a broken component doesn't affect the others, used in household wiring · Magnetism: magnets have a north pole and a south pole, like poles repel each other and unlike poles attract · Electromagnetism: an electric current always creates a magnetic field, which is used in electromagnets, motors and generators.
